title: The Pre-Cap Creative Audit
subtitle: Score whether your Meta creative can actually hold a bigger budget, before you raise the cap.

persona_selector.text: What are you spending on Meta right now?

questions.text: On mute, in the first 3 seconds, is it obvious what's being sold?
Does frame one show the product or the problem, not a logo intro?
Do you track thumb-stop rate (3s views / impressions) on cold traffic?

low.headline: Your hooks are losing the click before budget matters
low.text: On a 5x budget jump, a weak first 3 seconds gets punished, not rewarded. If a stranger can't tell what's being sold on mute, the spend just buys more scroll-past.
steps: Rewrite every hook so the product or problem is on-screen in second one
Cut logo intros and slow builds from the first 3 seconds
Pull thumb-stop rate per creative and cap anything under 30% on cold traffic

mid.headline: The hooks work, but not all of them hold at scale
mid.text: Some creatives stop the scroll and some coast on warm audiences. At higher spend the coasting ones bleed. Sort by thumb-stop before you raise a cap.
steps: Rank live creatives by thumb-stop rate, not by spend
Keep only hooks that clear your cold-traffic benchmark before scaling
Rebuild the middle of the pack instead of pushing budget through it

high.headline: Your hooks are built to survive a budget jump
high.text: Frame one earns the stop and the data backs it. Keep protecting the first 3 seconds as the thing you scale on.
steps: Keep thumb-stop rate as the first gate before any budget increase
Bank your winning hook patterns into a swipe file for the next batch
Test one new hook angle a week so the account never runs dry

questions.text: Does each ad carry one clear message instead of three at once?
Is there a single strong offer a cold stranger would act on?
Does the offer stay clear past the hook, not drop off after frame 1?

low.headline: Too many messages, no single reason to act
low.text: When an ad says three things it says nothing. A bigger budget just distributes the confusion faster. One ad, one message, one offer.
steps: Strip each ad to a single message a stranger repeats back
Put one strong offer in plain language, early
Cut secondary CTAs and 'also' lines that split attention

mid.headline: The message is clear, the offer isn't always sharp
mid.text: Your ads read cleanly but the offer sometimes hides. At scale the sharp-offer creatives carry the account, so make the offer impossible to miss.
steps: Lead with the offer, not the brand story
Test one stronger offer against your control before scaling spend
Make sure the promise in frame one survives to the CTA

high.headline: One message, one offer, holds all the way through
high.text: Your creatives make a single clear promise and keep it. That's what lets budget compound instead of leak.
steps: Keep the one-message rule as a hard gate on new creative
Rotate the offer angle before fatigue, not after
Document your best-performing offer framing for the next launch

questions.text: Do you run native, UGC-style creative, not just polished studio spots?
Are you feeding 3 to 4 strong concepts, not 20 near-identical cuts?
Are creatives built for placement (vertical, sound-off, mobile-first)?

low.headline: The algorithm doesn't have enough real variety to work with
low.text: Twenty versions of one studio spot is one bet, not a spread. Broad targeting needs genuinely different concepts to find the buyer.
steps: Add native, UGC-style creative next to the polished spots
Narrow to 3-4 distinct concepts, then vary within each
Cut variants that are the same idea in a new font

mid.headline: Decent spread, but a few formats do all the work
mid.text: You have variety, but placement fit and native creative are thin in spots. Fill those before you scale so the algorithm keeps options.
steps: Add a native/UGC concept to every scaling ad set
Build for the placement: vertical, legible sound-off, mobile-first
Retire look-alike variants that just split your data

high.headline: A real spread the algorithm can actually optimize
high.text: Distinct concepts, native formats, built for placement. That's the creative volume a bigger budget needs to stay efficient.
steps: Keep 3-4 live concepts and refresh one per week
Track which concept, not which variant, is winning
Feed new native angles before the current set fatigues

questions.text: Does the landing page repeat the ad's promise in the first screen?
Does the page load fast enough that the click survives?
Can a buyer tell within seconds they landed in the right place?

low.headline: You're paying for clicks the page then loses
low.text: A strong ad into a mismatched or slow page is money spent to bounce. At scale the leak is proportional to the budget.
steps: Make the landing headline echo the exact ad promise
Fix load speed before you raise spend, not after
Match the page's first screen to the creative a buyer just saw

mid.headline: The page mostly holds, but the scent trail breaks in places
mid.text: Some ads hand off cleanly and some drop the buyer into a generic page. Tighten the match on your scaling creatives first.
steps: Build a matched landing section per top creative angle
Audit load speed on mobile for your highest-spend ads
Keep the promise, proof and CTA above the fold

high.headline: Ad-to-page handoff is tight enough to scale on
high.text: The promise carries from creative to page and the page loads fast. That's what turns more spend into more buyers, not more bounce.
steps: Keep a matched page section for each scaling concept
Re-check mobile speed whenever you add budget
Test one stronger above-the-fold proof point per month

questions.text: Do you kill an ad when it stops working, not when you get bored?
Do you judge the account weekly, not by the daily panic?
Do you know the break-even ROAS a creative must clear before you raise the cap?

low.headline: You're scaling on gut, and gut breaks at $20k a day
low.text: Without kill rules and a break-even number, a budget bump is a guess. Guessing is what drains a small account and blows up a big one.
steps: Set a rule for when an ad gets killed, and follow it
Judge the account on a weekly cadence, not daily emotion
Calculate your break-even ROAS and treat it as the scaling gate

mid.headline: You have discipline, it's just not consistent yet
mid.text: You kill losers and check the numbers, but not on a system. At scale the discipline has to be a rule, not a mood.
steps: Write your kill and scale rules down and apply them the same way each week
Set a break-even ROAS per product and check creatives against it
Review weekly, decide weekly, stop reacting to daily swings

high.headline: You scale on signals, not nerves
high.text: Clear kill rules, weekly judgment, and a break-even number. That's the discipline that lets an account go from $1k to $20k a day without falling over.
steps: Keep the weekly review as the only place scaling decisions get made
Re-check break-even ROAS whenever COGS or shipping moves
Raise caps in steps the creative has already proven it can hold

cta.headline: Turn this score into creative that holds budget
cta.description: You can see where your creative would break under a bigger budget. The next step is a system that audits every creative before you scale and turns your best posts into content and lead magnets on autopilot. Book a 30-minute call and I'll show you where to start.
